page: UpCloud GPU-20xCPU-256GB-1xL4 is a GPU-accelerated server instance designed for workloads requiring dedicated graphics acceleration and substantial memory capacity. It features 20 vCPUs powered by an AMD EPYC 9575F processor built on the x86_64 architecture, operating at a base frequency of 2.0 GHz. The CPU configuration provides 20 physical cores with a single thread per core under a shared allocation model. This is paired with 256.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 12.8 GB per core. Acceleration is delivered via a single NVIDIA L4 GPU based on the Ada Lovelace architecture, equipped with 24 GB of VRAM. No local storage is bundled with this instance, and it includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark data indicates exceptional single-core capabilities, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance, Geekbench single-core scores, and single-threaded compression and decompression tasks all ranking in the top tier. Multi-core performance is also strong, placing in the top 25 percent for both stress-ng and Geekbench multi-core tests. Memory bandwidth presents a mixed profile: small-block cached reads perform in the top 25 percent, while large-block uncached reads and writes fall into the average category. Notably, the hardware excels in LLM inference, achieving top-tier performance for both prompt processing and text generation using small and medium models.

From a resource density perspective, this server offers a highly specialized hardware profile that balances a modern GPU with a generous memory allocation, making it qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-intensive acceleration tasks. However, the lack of bundled local storage represents a key tradeoff, requiring external storage attachments for data-heavy operations. The shared CPU allocation model may also introduce performance variability under sustained multi-tenant loads. Given these characteristics, the instance is highly suited for machine learning inference, image processing, text processing, and database operations, while also supporting general-purpose workloads that benefit from GPU acceleration.
